title: Lose about {ratePct}% of your weight a week
why: Losing slowly keeps more muscle. In one trial, athletes who lost slowly even added some.
found: Elite athletes who lost about 0.7% of their weight a week gained 2.1% lean mass and lost 31% of their fat. Those losing 1.4% a week lost 21% of their fat and their lean mass did not change. Across training studies, an energy deficit held back lean-mass gains, though strength still improved.
forYou: {kgPerWeek} kg a week is {ratePct}% of your {weightKg} kg, inside the 0.5 to 1% a week these studies and contest-prep guidance support.

title: The faster pace needs fat to spare
why: Fat stores can only release so much energy a day. Diet harder than that and the gap comes out of muscle.
found: A model built from underfeeding studies puts the most the fat store can supply at about 290 kJ (69 kcal) per kg of fat per day, and says a deficit beyond that takes fat-free mass straight away. It is a model, not a trial, so we plan under it, at 48.5 kcal per kg of fat.
forYou: With the fat you carry, the deepest deficit we plan is about {ceilingKcal} kcal a day, so the fastest pace offered to you is {ratePct}% a week.

title: Recomp keeps the deficit under 500 kcal
why: In training studies, a deficit of about 500 kcal a day was enough to stop muscle gains.
found: A meta-regression of resistance-training trials found an energy deficit of about 500 kcal a day prevented lean-mass gains, and the authors advise against deficits larger than that when muscle is the goal. Strength gains were not affected by the deficit.
forYou: Your recomp runs about {deficitKcal} kcal under maintenance, below that line, so building muscle while losing fat is still realistic.

title: Ease in at about {ratePct}% a week
why: If you already train, a small deficit can trim fat while your muscle keeps growing.
found: In a 10-week trial of 30 trained people on high protein, a moderate deficit lost 2.9 kg of fat and gained 1.0 kg of lean mass, while eating at maintenance lost 1.4 kg of fat and gained the same lean mass. The fat-loss difference between the two groups was not statistically significant.
forYou: You chose to ease in, so the scale moves about {kgPerWeek} kg a week. This is one small trial, so treat the pace as a best estimate.

title: For men, 10 to 15% body fat is the sweet spot
why: Raters liked men at moderate leanness and muscle best. The very leanest bodies did not score highest.
found: Across six studies, men with moderate muscularity were rated most attractive. When observers set fat and muscle on male bodies themselves, they chose levels within the healthy range. A 2025 study of 283 raters in three countries, using real DXA scans, reportedly found the peak at about 13 to 14% body fat.
forYou: Your goal of {goalBf}% is measured against that band. These are ratings of photos by mostly Western raters, not a promise about real life.

title: Natural muscle tops out near an FFMI of 25
why: In one study, drug-free athletes topped out at a muscle-for-height score of about 25, so goals past it are flagged.
found: Among 157 male athletes, the 74 who did not use steroids had fat-free mass indexes reaching a well-defined limit of 25.0, while many users went past it. The authors called the limit preliminary, and some people exceed it naturally.
forYou: Your goal works out to an FFMI of about {ffmi}. Near or past 25 we show it as uncommon, not impossible.

title: Build about {gainKgPerWeek} kg of muscle a week
why: Muscle grows slowly and slows each year you train, and people differ, so the time is a range.
found: In 49 trials, resistance training alone added about 1.1 kg of lean mass over roughly 13 weeks, and extra protein added about 0.3 kg more. Men gain more muscle in absolute terms, but women gain about the same relative to the muscle they start with. How fast gains slow over the years is our assumption, not a measurement.
forYou: From your training history and frame, about {gainKgPerWeek} kg a week, give or take about a third.

title: Build up to {ceilingBf}%, trim back to {floorBf}%
why: This range is your choice of how lean to stay. No study shows one range builds more muscle than another.
found: When 34 men overate by 40% for 8 weeks, those who started with more body fat gained more weight and more fat. In a trial of 61 trained adults, dieting in blocks with breaks and dieting straight through kept the same lean mass and strength, and the block dieters felt less hungry.
forYou: You chose the {routeName} way, so you build up to about {ceilingBf}% and trim back to {floorBf}%.

title: Women's plans stop at 22% body fat
why: Very lean women risk losing their period, so plans keep a safety margin above that point.
found: Female physique athletes measured off-season averaged 23.4% body fat by DXA. Among those not on hormonal contraception, 27% had no periods, against none of the regular gym-goers. The study is small and cross-sectional, so 22% is a safety margin, not a proven threshold.
forYou: The leanest your plan takes you is {floorBf}%.

title: Expect some fat with the muscle
why: Even a planned surplus adds fat alongside muscle. A bigger one adds more fat, not more muscle.
found: Elite athletes given a planned surplus gained more weight than those eating freely, but the extra was fat: fat mass rose 15% against 3%, and lean mass gains did not differ. An off-season review advises a surplus of about 10 to 20% and slower gains for advanced lifters.
forYou: Your plan assumes about {fatPerLean} kg of fat for every kg of muscle, so a build ends a little softer and the next trim takes it off.

title: Phases end on your weight, not a body-fat reading
why: Body-fat readings are too rough to see a few kilos of change. A weight trend can.
found: Even a DXA scan, repeated on consecutive days in 21 trained athletes, varied by about 1.3 kg of fat mass, and home body-fat scales are less precise still. In one man weighed daily for 26 years, weight varied by about 0.5% from one day to the next, small enough for a trend to show real change.
forYou: This phase ends when your weight trend reaches about {exitWeightKg} kg. You still see body fat, it just does not decide.

title: Decisions wait for a month of weigh-ins
why: A full month evens out water swings, including the menstrual cycle, before a phase is called done.
found: Across 612,613 menstrual cycles logged in an app, the average cycle was 29.3 days, so a 28-day average covers most of a cycle. On real smart-scale data, exponentially weighted averages were among the best ways to fill gaps between weigh-ins.
forYou: We need at least three weigh-ins over a week before showing a trend, and phase decisions use your last 28 days.

title: {sets} hard sets a week for {muscle}
why: More weekly sets grow more muscle, with smaller gains from each extra set at the top.
found: A 2026 analysis of 67 studies found more weekly sets meant more muscle and strength, with returns tapering, more so for strength. Counting sets where a muscle only assists as half a set fitted the data best. An earlier analysis put each extra weekly set at about 0.4% more growth.
forYou: {sets} sets a week is where your experience and choices put {muscle}. Sets where it only assists count as half.

title: Each muscle about twice a week
why: Splitting the same weekly sets over two days grows muscle at least as well as one big day.
found: An early analysis of 10 studies found training a muscle twice a week grew it more than once. A larger 2019 analysis of 25 studies found that with weekly sets matched, frequency made no meaningful difference. So frequency mainly helps you fit the sets in.
forYou: Your {daysPerWeek}-day plan trains most muscles twice a week, which spreads the sets into sessions you can finish.

title: Most sets in the 5 to 15 rep range
why: Light and heavy weights build similar muscle when sets are hard. Heavier sets build more top-end strength.
found: Across 21 studies with sets taken to failure, light loads (60% of max or less) and heavy loads built similar muscle, while heavy loads gave bigger one-rep-max gains.
forYou: Big barbell lifts sit at 5 to 10 reps for strength and size; isolation moves sit at 10 to 15.

title: Stop most sets a rep or three short of failure
why: Muscle grows more as sets get close to failure, but going all the way adds little.
found: Muscle growth improved as sets ended closer to failure, while strength gains were similar across a wide range of effort, though the authors call this exploratory. A separate analysis of 15 studies found no evidence that training to true failure beats stopping short.
forYou: Each block starts a few reps short of failure and edges closer each week, and any exercise done as a single set goes to failure.

title: {restMin} min rests on the big lifts
why: Resting more than a minute keeps your reps up. Past about 90 seconds, growth evens out.
found: A meta-analysis of 9 studies found a small growth benefit to resting more than 60 seconds, and no clear difference past 90. In trained men, 3-minute rests built more strength and thigh muscle than 1-minute rests. For maximum strength in trained lifters, a review favours rests over 2 minutes.
forYou: Your pace rests the big lifts for {restMin} minutes. A quicker pace trades a little growth for time.

title: A lighter week every {deloadEvery} weeks
why: A planned easier week lets fatigue clear. Coaches agree on it, but trials are few.
found: Expert coaches agree a deload is a planned stretch of reduced training to clear fatigue, and a practical review notes they are commonly placed every 4 to 8 weeks. In one trial, a full week off mid-programme did not change muscle growth but slightly reduced strength gains.
forYou: Your lighter week is the last of each {deloadEvery}-week block: about half the sets, same weights, more reps in reserve.

title: Your training stays the same while you cut
why: Cutting back sets during a diet did not help trained men keep muscle.
found: Trained men dieting for 6 weeks did either 5 or 3 sets per exercise. Thigh muscle thickness showed no difference between groups, and the small loss of lean mass was similar in both.
forYou: Your sets are the same in every phase. Only the food changes.

title: {proteinG} g of protein a day
why: Protein helps muscle grow, and you need more when eating less, so cuts get the most.
found: Across 49 trials, protein added about 0.3 kg of lean mass to training, with no further gain above about 1.6 g per kg of body weight a day (the top of its confidence range was 2.2). When lean athletes cut calories, a review of 6 studies put needs higher, at 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of lean mass.
forYou: {proteinG} g is about {proteinPerKg} g per kg of your weight. It rises as you get leaner on a cut, and never goes down.

title: Eat {calories} kcal, about {deficitKcal} under maintenance
why: A deficit big enough to lose fat, capped where studies saw muscle gains stop.
found: Across resistance-training trials, a deficit of about 500 kcal a day stopped lean-mass gains, while strength still improved. So no cut here asks for more than 500, and leaner people get less.
forYou: Your deficit is about {deficitKcal} kcal a day, which plans for about {kgPerWeek} kg a week.

title: Never below {floorKcal} kcal
why: Eating too little for your training disrupts hormones, so calories never drop under a floor set by your lean mass.
found: In 29 regularly menstruating women, hormone pulses were normal at 30 kcal per kg of lean mass a day and disrupted below it. That study was small, short and in women who did not exercise, and the IOC 2023 consensus treats low energy availability as a health risk for athletes.
forYou: Your floor is {floorKcal} kcal: 30 kcal per kg of your lean mass plus what your training burns. We apply it whatever your sex.

title: Maintenance of about {tdee} kcal
why: Your burn is estimated from your size, age, daily activity and training, so treat it as a starting point.
found: The Mifflin-St Jeor equation was built from measured resting energy in 498 adults. A systematic review found it predicted resting burn within 10% for more people than any other equation, but still with notable individual errors. Weight training is listed at 3.5 to 6.0 METs.
forYou: About {tdee} kcal from your body, your day and your training sessions. Your weigh-ins show whether it is right for you.

title: Eat about {surplusPct}% above maintenance
why: A small surplus feeds muscle growth. Eating more adds fat faster, not muscle.
found: Athletes given a bigger planned surplus gained more fat than those eating freely, with no difference in lean mass gained. An off-season review suggests about 10 to 20% over maintenance and gaining 0.25 to 0.5% of body weight a week, with advanced lifters going slower.
forYou: Your {surplusPct}% sits at or below that range, because the more training you have behind you, the less extra food you can turn into muscle.

why: Every recipe is added up from USDA values per 100 g of each ingredient, not guessed.
found: USDA's FoodData Central brings together lab-analysed foundation foods, the long-standing SR Legacy tables, survey foods and branded products, and aims to be reliable and transparent. Each ingredient here carries values per 100 g from it.
